html:
The Bengal Sultanate was an independent Muslim kingdom in the delta of the Ganges and Brahmaputra from 1352 to 1576. It was one of the richest states in Asia, known abroad for its rice and its cotton cloth.

Bengal had been conquered for Delhi about 1204 (see the Khalji conquest), but it was far away and its governors often rebelled. In 1352 Ilyas Shah united the region and made it a kingdom. Delhi tried twice to take it back and failed among the rivers.

The sultans ruled from Pandua and then Gaur. The Adina Mosque at Pandua, built in 1373, was the largest in the subcontinent. In 1414 a Bengal sultan sent a giraffe from East Africa to the emperor of China, and the fleets of Zheng He called at its ports. The silver coin was the taka, still the name of Bangladesh's money.

The sultans were foreigners by descent but ruled as Bengalis. Under Husain Shah, from 1494 to 1519, poets translated the Sanskrit epics into Bengali at court, and the saint Chaitanya preached freely.

Sher Shah took Bengal in 1538. Afghan rulers held it until the Mughal army of Akbar beat the last of them in 1576. See also Bengal.
sum: The Bengal Sultanate was an independent Muslim kingdom in the delta of the Ganges and Brahmaputra from 1352 to 1576. It was one of the richest states in Asia, known abroad for its rice and its cotton cloth.
